text:
This is Dr. Michael Ruscio (Healthy Gut, Healthy You) and Dr. Mark Pimentel (The Microbiome Connection): calm the inflammation down and starve the overgrowths, no harsh chemicals.

Diet-wise, go Paleo-Low FODMAP (Ruscio), which is low in the carbs your gut bacteria ferment most easily, or Low Fermentation Eating (Pimentel). Either way you stop feeding the bacteria in your small intestine.

And no snacking! Pimentel wants meals 4-5 hours apart, strictly, so the Migrating Motor Complex (MMC) gets to sweep your gut clean in between.
reader: Someone starting Phase 2's diet, to calm the inflammation and starve an overgrowth in the small intestine.

sentences.s: This is Dr. Michael Ruscio (Healthy Gut, Healthy You) and Dr. Mark Pimentel (The Microbiome Connection): calm the inflammation down and starve the overgrowths, no harsh chemicals.
Diet-wise, go Paleo-Low FODMAP (Ruscio), which is low in the carbs your gut bacteria ferment most easily, or Low Fermentation Eating (Pimentel).
sentences.payoff: The reader knows what a low-FODMAP diet cuts (the carbs gut bacteria ferment most), the reason it starves an overgrowth.
sentences.follows: It gives the diet after the phase's aim.

sentences.s: Either way you stop feeding the bacteria in your small intestine.
Pimentel wants meals 4-5 hours apart, strictly, so the Migrating Motor Complex (MMC) gets to sweep your gut clean in between.

checked.point: FODMAPs are the carbs gut bacteria ferment most easily
checked.found: short-chain carbohydrates, poorly absorbed and rapidly fermented (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23588241/)
checked.still_needed: yes: it says what the diet cuts

placement: Phase 2, the diet; the FODMAP note where the diet is named.

questions.Q1: PASS: each term note comes right where the term first appears, or in the next sentence, and the sentence's own point still comes first; the caution's instruction now follows its warning
questions.Q2: PASS: every instruction says what it is for in the reader's terms (take it away from meals so food doesn't compete; check with your oncologist before the 5g)
questions.Q3: PASS: each term note names the exact thing (the A1 type of casein protein; the seals between the cells of your gut lining; the first milk a cow makes after giving birth)
questions.Q4: PASS: each new "it", "that" and "this" has its object in the sentence before
questions.Q5: PASS: each "so", "but" and "because" has the claim it turns on said before it
questions.Q6: PASS: the notes sit where a reader first needs them; nothing moved except the caution's instruction, up to where a reader with cancer needs it
questions.Q7: PASS: each note helps this reader act on the sentence it explains
questions.Q8: PASS: no item moved between groups
questions.Q9: PASS: the long notes are their own short sentences (stress, colostrum, BPC-157), one step each

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first; a study after the question it answers)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
question_text.Q9: Is anything compressed? (one step a sentence, the small words that carry the relation, no space before mg)
